answer: About 700,000 Palestinian Arabs left or were driven from their homes in 1947 to 1949; Britannica says the figure likely exceeded 700,000. It happened inside a civil war and then a war with Arab armies. Morris documents expulsions from Lydda and Ramle in July 1948; many others fled in fear, and the UN mediator in 1948 named panic, rumours of terror and expulsion. Some wealthier families left from December 1947, before the main fighting. Historians weigh the causes differently: Morris finds no master plan but has himself used the words 'partial ethnic cleansing'; Khalidi calls it expulsion; Pappe, planned ethnic cleansing; Karsh blames mainly Arab leaders. In places such as Haifa, local Arab leaders ordered or advised leaving. Imseis says an Israeli cabinet decision of June 1948 barred return. Our reading: a fair answer does not deny expulsions or call them the only cause.

could_not_verify: A readable page with Erskine Childers's 1961 finding on Arab radio broadcasts, other than MERIP (advocacy). Not counted.
Pappe's 2006 Journal of Palestine Studies article: the PDF is blocked. His words are taken from a 2024 interview and an Al Jazeera quotation.

Morris's 1988 book and his 'Birth ... Revisited': no authorised readable copy. His own words come from the 2004 Los Angeles Times article (History News Network reprint), the 2004 Haaretz interview (first page read in a Wayback copy; the 'ethnic cleansing' exchange read in the Jewish Journal's reprint), his NYRB letter, and conference summaries.

Morris's phrase 'partial ethnic cleansing' (restored as a fact): the phrase itself appears only in the Los Angeles Times article, so only that record carries it. The Haaretz interview, the Reason piece and the NYRB exchange report that he accepted the term ('there are circumstances in history that justify ethnic cleansing') and say 'partial' only of expulsion; they do not repeat the phrase. Morris says the interviewer did not quote him in full; a person should read the whole Haaretz interview (Haaretz archive) and decide how it should be summarised. Contested keeps his reply.

Departures before the fighting reached people (restored as a fact): four sources (Morris in the Palestine-Israel Journal, a Christian Science Monitor review of his book, the Israel Law Review workshop summary, Karsh), but three carry Morris's own account; Karsh is the independent reading. The effect on later flight is contested, not asserted. A person should read Morris, The Birth of the Palestinian Refugee Problem Revisited, ch. 3, and the UN mediator's progress report on the early months.

The UN refugee office's counts: the Acting Mediator's report (472,000) and UNRWA's own page are the records read; Britannica and the Israel Law Review summary are the readers. The UN Conciliation Commission's own 1949-50 count is read only via the Israel Law Review summary.

Fact on the refugees' return: the UN mediator's report and Resolution 194 are records read directly, with the Israel Law Review and Imseis as readers. That the refugees were then not allowed back rests on Imseis alone (an Israeli cabinet decision of June 1948); I found no second readable source and no readable source for Israel's stated reasons (security, the Arab states' refusal of peace, the 1949 Lausanne offers). A person should read Morris on the cabinet decision and Israeli government statements of 1948-49.

Operation Hiram in detail: the scholarly chapter (Luminos) and the Journal of Palestine Studies article on a Galilean village were not readable (403). The autumn 1948 fact rests on the Israel Law Review summary of Morris and a Palestinian historian, Britannica and Imseis.
Whether the top-down expulsion order at Lydda is disputed by named historians: I did not find a readable page, so I did not claim it.
Primary documents for the Lydda and Ramle order (Rabin and Ben-Gurion diaries): no readable page.
Relabelled as 'other' (no named author or institution): History Skills.
Facts that do not meet the gate's source rule: the cabinet decision that barred return (one scholar).

FINAL REVIEW (2026-11-20): fact 1 was flagged as a record fact, but its four sources give four different counts (472,000; about 750,000; about 500,000; just over 700,000), so no two readers report the same content; I removed the record flag and the is_record marks, and it now rests on four reliable sources reporting different figures, each attributed. Fact 11: the phrase 'partial ethnic cleansing' is in the Los Angeles Times article only; Reason and the New York Review of Books report the Haaretz exchange, not that phrase, so the first half of the fact has the record and no reader. Fact 12 (return barred) rests on Imseis alone; the UN paper is cited twice and shows Israel's 1949 position, not the cabinet decision. The Commentary pages are now behind a login; the Karsh and letter quotes were read in Wayback copies and the card points to them.
not_claimed: This card does not deny that expulsions happened. It says they happened in specific places.
It does not claim all 700,000 were expelled, or that all fled voluntarily.
It does not claim the Arab radio-orders story is proven; the evidence on it is thin and disputed.
It does not address the right of return, property, or who is responsible for the refugees' present status.

skeptic.notes: Final review after the record rule. Read: the Acting Mediator's report (472,000; 'slightly over 500,000'), UNRWA's page (about 750,000), Bernadotte's report A/648 ('panic ... rumours ... or expulsion'; 'elemental justice'), Resolution 194, the CCP secretariat paper, Morris in the Los Angeles Times (HNN reprint) and in the Haaretz interview (Jewish Journal reprint, Reason, NYRB), Morris in the Palestine-Israel Journal and the Israel Law Review summary, the Christian Science Monitor review, and Karsh in Commentary (Wayback). Restored fact 11 (Morris's 'partial ethnic cleansing'): the LAT quote is exact and in context ('an element of the partial ethnic cleansing that rid Israel of the majority of its Arab inhabitants'; he also calls it inevitable, and the card says so); the Haaretz reply is exact, but it answers the interviewer's statement, not a question: fixed (should-fix, done). The record flag is honest in wording, but the LAT phrase has no reader, so that half rests on the record alone (should-fix; a person should read Morris's book or the full Haaretz interview). Restored fact 10 (departures before the fighting): fair and attributed to Morris and Karsh; three of its four sources carry Morris's own account (the PIJ talk, the ILR summary of a talk, a review of his book), so it is two voices, Morris and Karsh; worded as theirs, not as established (nit). Fixed by me: fact 1 record flag removed (must-fix, done; see could_not_verify); Commentary quotes made reachable through Wayback copies because the live pages are now paywalled and the online gate failed on them (must-fix, done). Still open: (must-fix) fact 12, return barred, has one reader (Imseis) and no source for Israel's stated reasons; (should-fix) fact 7 (autumn 1948) rests on Morris's talk, Imseis and a Britannica line that does not mention refugees; (should-fix) Britannica could not be read today (403); (nit) fact 9: the mediator's 'elemental justice' sentence has no reader.
